entries.question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate's conclusion is incorrect — the saga is sacrificed by state-based actions before triggered abilities are placed on the stack, so Eternal Witness's trigger can target Elspeth Conquers Death in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
No. Elspeth Conquers Death is still on the battlefield (not in Alec's graveyard) at the moment Eternal Witness's enters-the-battlefield trigger goes on the stack and its target must be chosen, so it can't be targeted.

Why: Elspeth Conquers Death's chapter III ability returns Eternal Witness during that ability's resolution. The Saga isn't sacrificed until after chapter III has resolved — that sacrifice is a separate triggered ability. Eternal Witness's trigger ("you may return target card from your graveyard to your hand") is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, and its target is chosen at that time [603.3d], [115.1d]. At that point Elspeth Conquers Death is either still on the battlefield or the sacrifice trigger is only just going on the stack alongside Eternal Witness's trigger; either way the card isn't in the graveyard yet, so it's not a legal target. Targets can't be changed afterward [115.1d], so once the Saga is sacrificed the trigger can't retroactively pick it up.

Contrast: Eternal Witness can target a card that was put into your graveyard during the resolution of the spell or ability that put Eternal Witness onto the battlefield [Eternal Witness ruling #0]. Elspeth Conquers Death doesn't go to the graveyard during chapter III's resolution, so that ruling doesn't help here.

Alec should instead target some other card in the graveyard (or decline, since the ability says "you may"). This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since only Alec's own permanent and graveyard are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

entries.question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Robber of the Rich lets Autumn spend {C} as though it were red to pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost (assuming spectacle's condition and timing are met).
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using one {C}, thanks to Robber of the Rich.

Why:

1. Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack that means "You may pay [cost] rather than this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" [702.137a]. Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost is {R} — a single red mana specifically, not generic. That cost is fixed regardless of how much life was lost or how many opponents lost life [Light Up the Stage ruling #7].

2. Robber of the Rich's own text says that during any turn you attacked with a Rogue, "you may cast that card and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." Robber of the Rich is itself a Rogue and attacked, so that permission applies to the exiled Light Up the Stage. An effect letting you spend mana as though it were mana of any color affects only how you pay the cost — it doesn't change the cost, and the mana spent is still actually {C} [609.4b]. So {C} can be spent as though it were {R} to pay the spectacle cost. This card-specific permission is what overrides the normal rule that {C} never satisfies {R}.

3. Autumn must announce the intention to use the alternative (spectacle) cost as part of proposing the spell, before costs are locked in [601.2b], [601.2f], and only one alternative cost/casting method may be applied to a spell [601.2b].

Two conditions still have to be met:
- An opponent must have lost life this turn [702.137a]. If no opponent has lost life at the time Autumn casts it, the spectacle cost isn't available and Autumn would owe {2}{R} instead (still payable with {C}-as-any-color mana via Robber of the Rich).
- Timing: spectacle doesn't change when the spell can be cast [Light Up the Stage ruling #8], and Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, so Autumn must cast it during their own main phase with an empty stack — practically, the postcombat main phase of this turn.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Autumn casts Light Up the Stage after combat damage in the postcombat main phase of the same turn Robber of the Rich attacked; if Autumn instead tried to cast it before any opponent had lost life, spectacle wouldn't be available yet and the full {2}{R} would be due.

Multiplayer note: spectacle only asks that *an* opponent lost life, so at a larger table life lost by any opponent — not necessarily Nehemiah, the defending player whose library was exiled — enables the spectacle cost. This works the same in a two-player game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Jinx overwrites Urza's Saga's land type, causing it to lose its chapter abilities and be immediately sacrificed for having no chapter abilities while still a Saga.
entries.answer:
Urza's Saga is immediately sacrificed by Nico. Jinx sets the land's subtype to a basic land type of Alexzander's choice; per 305.7, when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land type (Urza's Saga) and loses all abilities generated from its rules text and old land types, gaining only the mana ability of the new basic type. That strips its three chapter abilities. Setting a land subtype doesn't touch other card types or subtypes (205.1a, 205.4b), so the permanent is still an enchantment with the Saga subtype — a Saga with zero chapter abilities. Urza's Saga ruling #1 states directly that if Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed; the sacrifice state-based action (704.5s, 714.4) doesn't use the stack, so it happens as soon as Jinx resolves, before anyone gets priority.

Consequences: chapter III never triggers, so Nico gets no artifact tutor, and no lore counter is added on a later turn. Any ability Urza's Saga had already gained from chapters I and II (the {T}: Add {C} ability and the {2}, {T}: Construct token ability) was granted by another effect and would normally survive the subtype change (305.7, Urza's Saga ruling #5), but that's moot because the permanent leaves the battlefield right away. Nico could, in response to Jinx while it's still on the stack, activate the {2}, {T} Construct ability (or tap for {C}) to get value before Jinx resolves.

Timing note: I'm assuming Jinx resolves while Urza's Saga still has its chapter abilities and two lore counters, and that chapter III has not triggered. If instead Jinx resolves while a chapter ability of Urza's Saga has triggered and is still on the stack, that ability still resolves (it exists independently on the stack), and the sacrifice waits until it leaves the stack (714.4).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since Jinx targets a single land and the sacrifice is performed by that land's controller, Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

entries.question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that suspending Shade of Trokair is not casting (so it doesn't trigger Ethersworn Canonist) and Ada can then cast Divination, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ada can suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination, in that order.

Why: Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting. It doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to [116.2f, Shade of Trokair ruling #7, 702.62a]. So paying {W} to exile Shade of Trokair with three time counters does not make Ada a player who "has cast a nonartifact spell this turn," and Ethersworn Canonist's restriction is not switched on by it. Divination ({2}{U}, a sorcery) is then Ada's first nonartifact spell cast this turn, so Ethersworn Canonist permits it.

The one requirement to watch is the other direction: to take the suspend special action, Ada must be able to *begin to cast* Shade of Trokair from hand at that moment, taking into account any effect that prohibits casting it [702.62c, 601.3, Shade of Trokair ruling #2]. Shade of Trokair is a creature card, so that means Ada's main phase with an empty stack and priority [117.1a], and it means Ethersworn Canonist must not already be prohibiting Ada from casting nonartifact spells. Assuming (as the question implies) Ada has cast no nonartifact spell yet this turn, that's satisfied. Note it's only the *permission* to begin casting that matters — Ada doesn't have to be able to complete the cast [Shade of Trokair ruling #2].

If the order were reversed — Divination first — then Ethersworn Canonist would prohibit Ada from casting nonartifact spells for the rest of the turn, so Ada could no longer legally begin to cast Shade of Trokair and therefore could not take the suspend special action [702.62c, Shade of Trokair ruling #2].

Also note Ethersworn Canonist only looks at spells cast earlier in the turn, including before it entered the battlefield [Ethersworn Canonist ruling #0]. This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since Ethersworn Canonist's restriction is tracked separately for each player.

Later, when Shade of Trokair's last time counter is removed, Ada may cast it without paying its mana cost — but that is an actual cast, so Ethersworn Canonist would stop it if Ada had already cast a nonartifact spell that turn; if Ada declines or can't, Shade of Trokair stays exiled [702.62a, Shade of Trokair ruling #5].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Suspending a card is not casting a spell, so it does not count towards Ethersworn Canonist's restriction.

entries.question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
entries.reason: Both conclude it's legal — you may activate Inventors' Fair (its activation legality is checked before payments) and sacrifice Piston Sledge to Krark‑Clan Ironworks' mana ability to produce the mana needed to pay the {4} cost.
entries.answer:
Yes, it's legal — but only indirectly. Asa can't sacrifice a Piston Sledge as part of Inventors' Fair's cost itself; Inventors' Fair's ability reads "{4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair," so the only permanent sacrificed to that cost is Inventors' Fair. What Asa can do is sacrifice a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability ("Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}") to produce mana that pays the {4}.

Details:

- Legality check on activation: Inventors' Fair's ability says "Activate only if you control three or more artifacts." At the moment of activation Asa controls Krark-Clan Ironworks and two Piston Sledge — three artifacts (Inventors' Fair is a land, not an artifact), so the restriction is satisfied [601.3]. Per [Inventors' Fair ruling #2], the artifact count is checked only as the ability is activated, not again on resolution, so sacrificing artifacts afterward to pay costs doesn't invalidate it.
- Paying the {4}: Asa may activate Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability during the payment step, since a player may activate a mana ability whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment, even mid-activation [605.3a]. Each activation sacrifices one Piston Sledge and yields {C}{C}. {C} is colorless mana, which is a legal payment for generic mana, so two activations (sacrificing both Piston Sledge) fully pay the {4}; one activation only produces {C}{C}, and partial payments aren't allowed [601.2h], so Asa needs {4} total — the other {2} could come from another source, e.g. Inventors' Fair's own "{T}: Add {C}" is unavailable because the {T} is already part of the ability's cost and a tapped permanent can't be tapped again [118.3].
- One sacrifice, one cost: Sacrificing a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks pays Krark-Clan Ironworks' cost only; that same sacrifice can't also count as a cost of Inventors' Fair's ability [118.10].
- Total cost is locked in when the ability is activated, before payments are made [601.2f], so nothing about sacrificing artifacts afterward changes it.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here involves opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. It must be legal to activate the ability in order to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are only activated after the legality of activating the original ability has been checked.

entries.question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
entries.reason: Both conclude Psychogenic Probe does trigger (dealing 2 to Nico) because Progenitus’s replacement effect replaces the discard with a reveal-and-shuffle, so a shuffle occurred.
entries.answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Why: Pain resolving makes Nico discard a card. Progenitus has the static replacement ability "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead," so instead of going to Nico's graveyard, Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Nico's library. That shuffle is caused by an ability (Progenitus's own replacement ability), which is exactly what Psychogenic Probe looks for: "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player." The player who shuffled is Nico, so Nico takes the 2 damage, even though Amare controls Psychogenic Probe.

One timing note: the trigger event must actually happen for the ability to trigger (see rule 603.2g). Here it does — the shuffle is not prevented or replaced, it *is* the replacement. If some other effect had stopped Progenitus from being put into a graveyard at all (so no shuffle occurred), Psychogenic Probe would not trigger.

This works the same regardless of the number of players; Psychogenit Probe's damage simply goes to whichever player shuffled, here Nico. Note also that Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't help, because Psychogenic Probe's trigger doesn't target Progenitus, and Progenitus is no longer the object being affected — Nico is the one dealt damage (compare Progenitus ruling #1: effects that don't target it can still affect it).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

entries.question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Ajani gains 2 counters by applying only Pir, but the correct result is 4 counters because Pir makes the +1 into two and Doubling Season then doubles those counters.
entries.answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains 2 loyalty counters, not 4.

Why Doubling Season doesn't apply: the [+1] in the ability's cost is loyalty counters put on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes as a *cost*, not as an effect. Doubling Season only replaces counters that an *effect* would put on a permanent you control, so it does nothing here (Doubling Season ruling #4 says exactly this: activating an ability whose cost has you put loyalty counters on a planeswalker is not doubled).

Why Pir, Imaginative Rascal does apply: Pir's text is not limited to effects — it reads "If one or more counters would be put on a permanent your team controls, that many plus one of each of those kinds of counters are put on that permanent instead." Card text governs over the general expectation, so the one loyalty counter paid as the cost becomes 1 + 1 = 2 loyalty counters on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes.

Side note on the ability's actual effect: the first +1 of Ajani, Mentor of Heroes distributes three +1/+1 counters among one to three target creatures you control, with the distribution announced on activation and each target getting at least one counter (Ajani, Mentor of Heroes ruling #1). Those +1/+1 counters ARE put on by an effect, so both Doubling Season and Pir, Imaginative Rascal apply to them; as the affected permanents' controller, Albert chooses the order the two replacement effects apply (616.1a, 616.1g). Applying Pir, Imaginative Rascal first and then Doubling Season is better: a creature slated for 1 counter gets (1+1)×2 = 4, versus (1×2)+1 = 3 the other way.

Timing/ambiguity note: I'm assuming both Doubling Season and Pir, Imaginative Rascal were already on the battlefield when the ability was activated. If Pir, Imaginative Rascal arrived only after the cost was paid, the loyalty payment would be just 1 counter.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on player count; Pir's "your team" matters only in team formats, and Doubling Season/Pir apply the same at a two-player or multiplayer table. APNAP order (101.4) for simultaneous replacement choices only comes up if multiple players must choose at once.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

entries.question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
entries.reason: The candidate says the Aura can enter attached and give Nico control of Haru-Onna, while the reference states that's not possible because Domestication can't be put onto the battlefield attached to a permanent entering simultaneously.
entries.answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell puts both permanents onto the battlefield at the same time, each under the control of the player who put it there (rule 110.2a, and the Aura enters already attached — 303.4e). The instant Domestication is on the battlefield, its continuous effect "You control enchanted creature" is applied in layer 2, the control-changing layer (613.1b), and Nico is Domestication's controller. Because Domestication entered simultaneously with Haru-Onna, Haru-Onna is under Nico's control from the moment it's on the battlefield — Aminah never has a moment of control after the event.

Haru-Onna's "When this creature enters, draw a card" then triggers on that event. A triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered (113.8, 603.3a, 109.4b). Since Nico controlled Haru-Onna at that time, Nico puts the ability on the stack and "draw a card" refers to Nico. Note also that Haru-Onna's second ability ("Whenever you cast a Spirit or Arcane spell...") likewise now belongs to Nico as the enchanted creature's controller, per 303.4e.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as both permanents entering simultaneously during Show and Tell's resolution, as the card's wording dictates. If instead Domestication somehow arrived later (e.g., cast afterward), Haru-Onna's ETB trigger would already have triggered and resolved under Aminah's control, and Aminah would draw the card.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, where each additional player may also put a permanent onto the battlefield under their own control.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

entries.question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Fatal Push won't destroy Skyhunter Patrol, but the reference correctly states the saga's state-based checks/sacrifice will create Revolt before Fatal Push resolves, so the creature will be destroyed.
entries.answer:
Yes, Amani can legally target Skyhunter Patrol with Fatal Push, but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Targeting: Fatal Push says only "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The mana-value clause is a condition on the destruction, not a restriction on what may be targeted, so any creature on the battlefield is a legal target — even one with mana value 5 or greater [Fatal Push ruling #3]. Creatures on the battlefield are legal targets for spells generally [115.2].

Resolution: Fatal Push's mana value check happens only as Fatal Push resolves [Fatal Push ruling #3]. Skyhunter Patrol has mana value 4 ({2}{W}{W}). Without Revolt, the effect only destroys the target if its mana value is 2 or less, so the "if" condition fails and nothing happens to Skyhunter Patrol. Note Skyhunter Patrol is still a legal target the whole time, so Fatal Push does resolve (it isn't removed from the stack as it would be with all targets illegal [608.2b]); it simply does nothing and then goes to Amani's graveyard as the final part of its resolution [608.2n]. Because Amani lacks Revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn), the "mana value 4 or less" version doesn't apply.

A couple of practical points on the Founding the Third Path chapter III: the Fatal Push card is exiled and Amani casts a copy, and Amani must pay the copy's full cost, {B}, and must cast it right then during the ability's resolution — Amani can't hold it for later [Founding the Third Path ruling #2].

If Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent, targeting it commits a crime [700.13][Crime]. That's true whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here changes with more players, except that in multiplayer Amani could instead target a creature controlled by any opponent (or their own).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

entries.question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Soldevi Digger becomes a colorless 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities and Bludgeon Brawl does not apply while it is a creature.
entries.answer:
After Titania's Song resolves, Soldevi Digger is a colorless 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger with no abilities and no subtypes (it is not an Equipment).

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1a, 613.6, 613.7, 613.8):

- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Bludgeon Brawl has the earlier timestamp, but Titania's Song applies first here by dependency. Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact," and Titania's Song's layer-4 part turns Soldevi Digger into an artifact creature — that changes what Bludgeon Brawl applies to, which is exactly the CR 613.8a dependency test, and dependency overrides timestamps (CR 613.8). So Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger an artifact creature, and Bludgeon Brawl then no longer applies to it at all: no Equipment subtype.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Since Bludgeon Brawl doesn't apply, it grants no equip {2} and no "Equipped creature gets +X/+0." Titania's Song removes all abilities, so Soldevi Digger loses "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library."
- Layer 7b (P/T setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2} (two generic), so its mana value is 2 — it's 2/2. Note mana value is a copiable printed characteristic and isn't changed by these effects.
- Color (CR 105.2): Soldevi Digger's mana cost {2} contains no colored mana symbols and nothing gives it a color, so it stays colorless.

Order assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield when Titania's Song resolved, as stated. If instead Titania's Song had been in play first and Bludgeon Brawl entered later, the answer is the same — the dependency (not the timestamp) drives the result, so Bludgeon Brawl still never applies while Soldevi Digger is a creature.

Also note Titania's Song's own text: "If this enchantment leaves the battlefield, this effect continues until end of turn" — that card text controls over the usual expectation that the effect ends immediately, so Soldevi Digger would remain a 2/2 ability-less artifact creature through end of turn. Only once that ends (and Soldevi Digger is a noncreature artifact again) would Bludgeon Brawl start applying, making it an Equipment with equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0."

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, and only Ari's permanents are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

entries.question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Enlarge's bonus ends while the -1/-1 counters remain, killing Goblin Piker at cleanup and triggering Baron Sengir's ability.
entries.answer:
At the cleanup step, Goblin Piker dies; Baron Sengir survives.

Step by step:

1. Sizes during combat. Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample until end of turn (layer 7 power/toughness effects, [613.1g]). Grafted Exoskeleton makes Baron Sengir 7/7 with infect, and Withstand Death gives Baron Sengir indestructible until end of turn.

2. Combat damage. Goblin Piker assigns 7 (lethal) to Baron Sengir and, with trample, the remaining 2 to Nico (2 life loss — Goblin Piker has no infect). Baron Sengir is indestructible, so the 7 marked damage doesn't destroy it. Baron Sengir has infect, so its 7 damage to Goblin Piker isn't marked; instead Nico puts seven -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker ([702.90c], [120.3]). Goblin Piker is then effectively 2/1 (9/8 minus seven) and lives through combat.

3. End of turn (cleanup step). All marked damage is removed and all "until end of turn"/"this turn" effects end simultaneously ([514.2]). Enlarge's +7/+7 and Withstand Death's indestructible both end at that moment. Baron Sengir loses indestructible but its marked damage is gone at the same time, so it's a fine 7/7 (5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton). Goblin Piker, however, keeps its seven -1/-1 counters — counters are not "until end of turn" effects — so it becomes 2/1 minus 7/7 = -5/-6. When state-based actions are checked, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration can't save it ([704.5f]).

4. Baron Sengir's ability. Goblin Piker was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn and it dies, so Baron Sengir's triggered ability meets its condition. The provided rules don't include the rule governing triggers during the cleanup step, so I can't state from this context exactly how that trigger is put on the stack — but the intent is that a +2/+2 counter goes on Baron Sengir.

Timing note: I'm assuming Withstand Death and Grafted Exoskeleton were already applied before combat damage. If Withstand Death were instead cast after damage was already marked, the result is the same, since indestructible only needs to be there when the destruction would happen and marked damage clears in the same cleanup event.

Player count: only Nico, the defending player, is affected here, so the answer is identical in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Skullbriar is exiled by Ghastly Conscription, keeps its +1/+1 counters from the graveyard, and is prevented from entering the battlefield by Containment Priest, leaving it in exile with its counters.
entries.answer:
All of the creature cards, including Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, end up exiled and none of them ever hit the battlefield.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription resolves and exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile (this is part of the spell's effect, not a state-based action), shuffles that pile, then tries to manifest those cards. Because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave still has its ability "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library" while it is in the graveyard — the zone it's moving from — it keeps its two +1/+1 counters as it goes to exile [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. Card text like this overrides the general expectation that counters fall off on a zone change.

2. Manifesting means putting the card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature. Those cards are nontoken creatures that are entering the battlefield without being cast, so Containment Priest's replacement ability applies: each one is exiled instead. Nothing manifested was cast, so the exception in [Containment Priest ruling #1] for cast creatures doesn't help here.

3. So Skullbriar, the Walking Grave never actually enters the battlefield; it simply stays in exile (now face up or face down per the exile effect's mechanics, but in either case not on the battlefield). Any effect that had been keyed to "for as long as it has a counter on it" would already have stopped applying, since Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a new object in each new zone even though it retains its counters [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3], and it retains all counters, not just +1/+1 ones [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5]. Those counters still set its power and toughness in nonbattlefield zones, so it is a 3/3 object in exile [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Containment Priest is already on the battlefield when Ghastly Conscription resolves (the question says Ashley controls it and then casts the sorcery). If Containment Priest were only cast with flash after Ghastly Conscription had already finished resolving and manifesting, the manifested creatures would already be on the battlefield and would not be exiled.

Multiplayer note: this works the same whether the game is two players or more; Ghastly Conscription targets one player (Niko), and Containment Priest's ability applies to any nontoken creature entering, regardless of controller or player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that when Putrid Leech stopped being revealed and later returned to the top it became a new object, so Skill Borrower gains a distinct, identically worded activated ability that can be activated again.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can activate the pumping ability again this turn.

Why: Skill Borrower grants Ashley's creature "all activated abilities" of the top card of the library while that card is an artifact or creature card, so with Putrid Leech on top, Skill Borrower has "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn." That "only once each turn" restriction is part of the ability as acquired from that particular object, and by rule 602.5c a restriction acquired from another object applies only to that ability as acquired from that object — it does not apply to other, identically worded abilities.

The key step is rule 401.6: because Ashley plays with the top card of their library revealed (Skill Borrower's first ability), when Putrid Leech stopped being revealed (it went second from the top after the first Sensei's Divining Top activation) and then was revealed again on top after the second Sensei's Divining Top activation, it became a new object. Skill Borrower therefore now has an identically worded but distinct acquired ability from a different object, and the earlier activation doesn't restrict it.

Timing notes: while Ashley is actually activating the ability, changes to the top card don't matter — Skill Borrower ruling #4 confirms that if the top card changes mid-activation, the ability is still activated and resolves normally, and rule 401.5 says a new top card isn't revealed until the activation is complete. Also note Sensei's Divining Top's second ability isn't in play here; only its first ability ({1}: look at the top three and reorder) was used, twice.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Putrid Leech stopped being revealed for a time, so it is no longer the same object that it was before. Skill Borrower has a new ability that just has the same text as the ability that was activated earlier.

entries.question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Spider Umbra's replacement effect applies to prevent the creature's destruction, destroying the Umbra instead and leaving Mons's Goblin Raiders on the battlefield (so Yamabushi's Flame's exile doesn't occur).
entries.answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives. Spider Umbra makes it a 2/2, so Yamabushi's Flame's 3 damage is lethal damage, and Mons's Goblin Raiders would be destroyed — but umbra armor replaces that: all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra is destroyed instead ([702.89a], [Spider Umbra ruling #6]). Mons's Goblin Raiders is not exiled, because Yamabushi's Flame's exile clause only applies to a creature that would actually die, and Mons's Goblin Raiders never dies.

Details: "Umbra armor" is a static ability meaning "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" ([702.89a]). It is a mandatory replacement effect that acts as a shield, applying as the event would happen ([614.1], [Spider Umbra ruling #6]). It applies no matter why the creature would be destroyed, including lethal damage ([Spider Umbra ruling #4]); when it's lethal damage rather than a "destroy" instruction, it's the game's lethal-damage rules that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed, not Yamabushi's Flame itself ([Spider Umbra ruling #0]). The damage is still dealt and marked, then processed into its result ([120.4c]); the destruction result is replaced, so damage is removed instead and Mons's Goblin Raiders ends up a 2/2 with no damage marked — until Spider Umbra leaves, at which point it's a 1/1 with no damage marked, so no toughness-0 state-based action applies ([704.5f]).

Note that Spider Umbra's own text ("instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura") overrides the normal outcome that lethal damage destroys the creature.

This interaction is between two specific players and doesn't depend on player count; it plays out identically at a two-player or multiplayer table. If Mons's Goblin Raiders had multiple umbra armor Auras, Noah would choose exactly one to be destroyed ([Spider Umbra ruling #7]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Carrion Grub becomes part of Alex’s library for the restarted game and therefore violates Kaheera’s companion restriction so Alex cannot have Kaheera as their companion.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: The game immediately ends with no winner or loser, and everyone still in the game starts a new game. Carrion Grub, which Alex brought in from outside the game with Wish, is now "involved in the game," so it becomes part of Alex's library for the new game (727.2). Because Alex's starting deck for the new game now contains Carrion Grub — an Insect, which is not a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast — Alex's deck no longer meets Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion requirement, so Alex cannot name Kaheera, the Orphanguard as companion in the new game (Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion text; Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0, ruling #10, 702.139b).

Details:
- Restarting: the old game ends immediately, no one wins, loses, or draws it, and all players still in the game begin a new game using the normal pregame procedure of rule 103 (727.1, 104.6, Karn Liberated ruling #12). Nothing that happened in the old game carries over — no counters, emblems, or lingering effects (Karn Liberated ruling #1, ruling #10).
- Carrion Grub: 727.2 states that all Magic cards involved in the ended game are involved in the new game, even if they weren't originally in it, and ownership doesn't change; the rule's own example (a creature brought in with Living Wish) says the card is part of that player's library when the new game begins. So Carrion Grub is shuffled into Alex's new library, not returned to the sideboard.
- Kaheera, the Orphanguard: it began the old game outside the game (sideboard), and "starting deck" means your deck after setting aside sideboard cards (702.139b, Kaheera ruling #10). Two timing cases: (1) If Alex never took the special action to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into hand, it is still outside the game; Alex may again reveal a companion before shuffling for the new game, but Kaheera, the Orphanguard's requirement fails because Carrion Grub is now in the starting deck. Alex may still simply include Kaheera, the Orphanguard in the deck as a normal card — the companion ability then does nothing and imposes no restriction (Kaheera ruling #7). (2) If Alex had already paid {3} to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into hand (or it was on the battlefield/in the graveyard), it was in the game (702.139c, Kaheera ruling #11, ruling #14), so under 727.2 it too becomes part of Alex's library for the new game and likewise can't be a companion.
- Karn Liberated's own text overrides the general restart procedure for cards it exiled: non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated stay in exile through the restart and are then put onto the battlefield under Alex's control. That happens after the pregame procedure but just before the first turn's untap step, with no player having priority; resulting triggers go on the stack at the first upkeep (727.4, 727.5, Karn Liberated ruling #4).
- Player count: with exactly two players, both start the new game. With more than two, every player still in the game when it restarted is in the new game, but anyone who had already left does not return (Karn Liberated ruling #11), and if the game used the limited range of influence option all players are involved regardless of range (727.7). The starting player for the new game is chosen by the normal rule‑103 procedure (103.1).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Carrion Grub will be shuffled into Alex's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Carrion Grub violates Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion restriction, Alex can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.
